strengths: The paper addresses a relevant NLP reliability problem: predicting answer failure before generation. A lightweight probe over frozen question representations offers a practical approach without updating the underlying LLM.

Table 1 provides encouraging evidence that question representations predict short-answer success across three LLMs and three datasets. FacLens generally matches or exceeds full fine-tuning while requiring substantially less training computation.

The reported cross-model adaptation gains are substantial: LLaMA2-to-LLaMA3 transfer on PopQA improves from 0.443 to 0.842 AUC. The additional Gemma experiment usefully examines transfer between models with different representation dimensions.

The paper includes useful analyses of layers, token pooling, entity representations, training size, and batch alignment. The matched-dataset-size experiment and explicit acknowledgment of weaker Natural Questions performance help characterize the method’s limits.
weaknesses: The central inference that successful pooled training establishes an absence of concept shift is not justified (Section 5.1). A pooled MLP can implement different predictors in separable model-specific representation regions. Moreover, equal AUC does not imply equal conditional probabilities, because AUC measures ranking rather than calibration. Comparing fitted probes in Figure 4 does not resolve these issues. Equation 7 likewise asserts a strict improvement from question alignment without establishing assumptions under which that inequality holds.

Label validity is insufficiently established. Exact substring matching can reject correct paraphrases or unlisted aliases and accept answers that mention the gold answer in an incorrect context. The manual audit covers only 180 examples labeled factual, leaving errors in the non-factual class unmeasured; short answers do not guarantee that class is correctly labeled. Counting refusals as non-factual is consistent with the stated failure-to-answer definition, but limits interpretation as hallucination detection or evidence of intrinsic knowledge.

The paired-question transfer setting lacks a crucial baseline: training a probe on target-model representations using the available source-model labels for those same questions. Reporting source–target label agreement and performance on questions where the models disagree would help distinguish model-specific prediction from shared question difficulty. A question-text baseline and a linear question-state probe under matched supervision, with comparison to the closely related work [18], would further establish what the proposed components contribute.

The unsupervised evaluation is not sufficiently reproducible. Appendix D does not specify how transfer checkpoints and kernels are selected without target labels, while Figures 6 and 10 plot target-test AUC throughout training. The selection protocol needs clarification. Exact answer-generation prompts, chat formatting, random seeds, and whether question splits are synchronized across LLMs are also unspecified. These details materially affect both the labels and the transfer results.

The strongest results come from random splits of template-based datasets. Natural Questions contains only 1,244 filtered examples, with middle-layer FacLens achieving approximately 0.69–0.71 AUC. The matched-size control is useful, but does not establish the proposed explanation involving removal of semantic information or the claim that middle layers 'know whether they know.' Repeated-run uncertainty and held-out-topic controls are missing. AUC alone also does not validate the probability estimates or deployment thresholds. Together with the central transfer and reproducibility concerns, these issues require important revisions before a Findings recommendation.
